skeletal muscle.name: Skeletal muscle
skeletal muscle.what: Long, cylindrical, multinucleated fibers with obvious cross-striations; nuclei lie at the periphery, just under the sarcolemma.
skeletal muscle.where: Skeletal muscles of the limbs and trunk, tongue, diaphragm, extraocular muscles and upper esophagus.
skeletal muscle.fn: Strong, quick, voluntary contraction under somatic motor control; responds to increased load by hypertrophy and regenerates only to a limited extent, using satellite cells.

cardiac muscle.name: Cardiac muscle
cardiac muscle.what: Branching, striated cells joined end to end at intercalated discs; each cell has one central nucleus.
cardiac muscle.where: Myocardium of the heart and the walls of the great veins where they enter the heart.
cardiac muscle.fn: Automatic, involuntary pumping. Contraction begins at the pacemaker nodes and spreads through gap junctions; regeneration is very poor.

smooth muscle.name: Smooth muscle
smooth muscle.what: Small fusiform (tapered) cells with a single central nucleus at the widest part of the cell and no cross-striations, because the contractile proteins are randomly arranged.
smooth muscle.where: Walls of blood vessels, the digestive and respiratory tracts, uterus, bladder and other hollow organs.
smooth muscle.fn: Slow, partial, often spontaneous wavelike involuntary contraction under autonomic control; can respond to load by both hypertrophy and hyperplasia and regenerates well.

striations.name: Striations (cross-striations)
striations.what: Alternating dark A bands and light I bands seen in longitudinal section, produced by the orderly in-register arrangement of sarcomeres.
striations.where: Skeletal and cardiac muscle only; absent from smooth muscle.
striations.fn: They are the optical signature of linearly arranged contractile proteins, which is what allows a strong, rapid, directional contraction.

muscle fiber.name: Muscle fiber
muscle fiber.what: A single skeletal muscle cell, 10–100 µm across and up to several centimetres long, packed with myofibrils and bounded by the sarcolemma.
muscle fiber.where: Throughout skeletal muscle, bundled into fascicles.
muscle fiber.fn: The contractile unit of a skeletal muscle; it is multinucleated because it forms by fusion of many myoblasts.

nuclei peripheral.name: Peripheral nuclei
nuclei peripheral.what: Multiple flattened nuclei pressed against the inner face of the sarcolemma.
nuclei peripheral.fn: Their peripheral position is the quickest way to tell skeletal muscle from cardiac muscle, whose nucleus is central.

nucleus central.name: Central nucleus
nucleus central.what: A single nucleus lying in the middle of the cell, often with a pale perinuclear zone of glycogen.
nucleus central.where: Cardiac muscle cells and smooth muscle cells.
nucleus central.fn: Central position plus branching and intercalated discs identifies cardiac muscle; central position in a fusiform cell with no striations identifies smooth muscle.

intercalated disc.name: Intercalated disc
intercalated disc.what: A step-like junction between adjacent cardiac muscle cells made of many junctional complexes: transverse portions carry desmosomes and fascia adherens, longitudinal portions carry gap junctions.
intercalated disc.fn: The transverse parts hold the cells together mechanically against constant beating; the longitudinal gap junctions form electrical synapses so the myocardium contracts as a functional syncytium.

connective tissue muscle.name: Connective tissue of muscle
connective tissue muscle.what: Three sheaths: endomysium around each fiber, perimysium around each fascicle, epimysium around the whole muscle.
connective tissue muscle.where: Skeletal muscle. Cardiac muscle has endomysium plus subendocardial and subpericardial layers; smooth muscle has endomysium and less organized sheaths.
connective tissue muscle.fn: Carries the vessels and nerves and transmits the force of contraction to the tendon.

sarcomere.name: Sarcomere
sarcomere.what: The segment of a myofibril between two Z discs; the repeating unit that gives striated muscle its banding.
sarcomere.fn: The functional contractile unit: during contraction the thin filaments slide toward the M line, the I band and H zone narrow and the Z discs come closer, while the A band stays the same length.

z disc.name: Z disc (Z line)
z disc.what: A dense transverse line bisecting each I band where thin (actin) filaments of neighbouring sarcomeres are anchored.
z disc.where: Boundary of every sarcomere in skeletal and cardiac muscle; in cardiac muscle the T tubules lie at the Z disc.
z disc.fn: Anchors the thin filaments and transmits tension from sarcomere to sarcomere. Z discs move closer together as the muscle shortens.

a band.name: A band
a band.what: The dark band, the full length of the thick (myosin) filaments, including the region where thin filaments overlap them.
a band.fn: Because it equals the length of the thick filament, the A band does NOT change length during contraction — a classic exam point.

i band.name: I band
i band.what: The light band containing only thin filaments, bisected by the Z disc.
i band.fn: Narrows during contraction as thin filaments slide inward.

h zone.name: H zone
h zone.what: The paler central part of the A band containing thick filaments only, with no thin filament overlap; the M line runs through its centre.
h zone.fn: Narrows and can disappear in a fully contracted sarcomere.

m line.name: M line
m line.what: A fine dark line in the middle of the H zone where thick filaments are cross-linked to one another.
m line.fn: Holds the thick filaments in register; the thin filaments are pulled toward it during the working stroke.

myofibril.name: Myofibril
myofibril.what: A long cylindrical bundle of myofilaments running the length of the fiber; myofibrils are composed of myofilaments, and the fiber is composed of myofibrils.
myofibril.where: Cytoplasm of skeletal and cardiac muscle cells.
myofibril.fn: Aligning the sarcomeres of neighbouring myofibrils in register produces the cross-striations and lets the whole fiber shorten together.

thick filament.name: Thick filament (myosin)
thick filament.what: Myosin II molecules with projecting heads; defines the A band.
thick filament.fn: The head binds actin, releases ADP and Pi during the working stroke, detaches when new ATP binds, and is re-cocked as ATP is split.

thin filament.name: Thin filament (actin)
thin filament.what: F-actin with tropomyosin and the troponin complex, anchored at the Z disc.
thin filament.where: Extends from each Z disc toward the centre of the sarcomere.
thin filament.fn: Troponin C binds Ca²⁺, which moves tropomyosin and exposes the actin sites for myosin binding — the switch that starts skeletal and cardiac contraction.

t tubule.name: T tubule (transverse tubule)
t tubule.what: A tube-like invagination of the sarcolemma that penetrates deep into the fiber.
t tubule.where: Skeletal muscle: at the A–I junction, forming triads with two terminal cisterns. Cardiac muscle: at the Z disc, forming dyads with one cistern. Smooth muscle has none, though caveolae may be functionally similar.
t tubule.fn: Carries the depolarization from the surface into the centre of the fiber so that all sarcomeres are triggered at once.

sarcoplasmic reticulum.name: Sarcoplasmic reticulum
sarcoplasmic reticulum.what: Specialized smooth ER forming a network around each myofibril, with terminal cisterns next to the T tubules.
sarcoplasmic reticulum.where: Skeletal muscle (well developed, two terminal cisterns per sarcomere in triads); cardiac (less developed, dyads); smooth muscle (irregular, without distinctive organization).
sarcoplasmic reticulum.fn: Stores and releases the Ca²⁺ that initiates contraction, then pumps it back to allow relaxation.

triad.name: Triad
triad.what: One T tubule flanked by two terminal cisterns of sarcoplasmic reticulum.
triad.where: At the A–I junction in skeletal muscle. Cardiac muscle has dyads instead.
triad.fn: The site where the voltage change in the T tubule is converted into Ca²⁺ release from the SR.

neuromuscular junction.name: Neuromuscular junction (motor end plate)
neuromuscular junction.what: The synapse between a terminal axonal twig and a skeletal muscle fiber, with the end plate embedded in a groove in the external lamina of the fiber.
neuromuscular junction.fn: ACh released from the axon terminal crosses the synaptic cleft and binds receptors on the highly folded sarcolemma, depolarizing the fiber and triggering contraction.

motor end plate.name: Motor end plate (MEP)
motor end plate.what: The expanded terminal of a motor axon branch sitting in a shallow groove on the muscle fiber; stains densely with silver.
motor end plate.where: Skeletal muscle fibers, usually near the middle of the fiber.
motor end plate.fn: The presynaptic half of the neuromuscular junction; one motor axon branches to supply many fibers, together forming a motor unit.

nerve bundle.name: Nerve bundle (NB)
nerve bundle.what: The parent motor nerve before it divides into terminal axonal twigs.
nerve bundle.where: Running through the endomysium and perimysium of skeletal muscle.
nerve bundle.fn: Delivers the motor axons that will each form a motor end plate on a muscle fiber.

axon terminal.name: Axon terminal
axon terminal.what: The swollen end of the motor axon, capped by a Schwann cell and filled with mitochondria and synaptic vesicles.
axon terminal.where: Presynaptic side of the neuromuscular junction.
axon terminal.fn: Depolarization opens Ca²⁺ channels at the active zones and vesicles release ACh into the cleft.

synaptic vesicle.name: Synaptic vesicles
synaptic vesicle.what: Small clear vesicles containing acetylcholine clustered at the active zones.
synaptic vesicle.where: Axon terminal of the neuromuscular junction.
synaptic vesicle.fn: Fuse with the presynaptic membrane to release ACh by exocytosis.

synaptic cleft.name: Synaptic cleft
synaptic cleft.what: The narrow space, containing external lamina, between the axon terminal and the sarcolemma.
synaptic cleft.fn: ACh diffuses across it; acetylcholinesterase in the cleft then destroys the transmitter so the signal is brief.

junctional folds.name: Junctional folds
junctional folds.what: Deep infoldings of the postsynaptic sarcolemma beneath the axon terminal.
junctional folds.where: Postsynaptic membrane of the motor end plate.
junctional folds.fn: Greatly increase the membrane area and therefore the number of ACh receptors, making transmission reliable.

ach receptor.name: ACh receptor region of sarcolemma
ach receptor.what: The folded postsynaptic membrane packed with nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
ach receptor.fn: Receptor binding opens cation channels, depolarizes the sarcolemma and initiates the muscle action potential; blocked in myasthenia gravis by autoantibodies.

schwann cell.name: Schwann cell
schwann cell.what: A glial cell that caps the axon terminal and myelinates the axon up to the terminal.
schwann cell.where: Peripheral nerves, including the motor axon at the NMJ.
schwann cell.fn: Myelinates the axon for fast conduction and covers the terminal, isolating the synapse.

endomysium capillary.name: Endomysial capillary network
endomysium capillary.what: A rich plexus of capillaries running in the endomysium along and around individual muscle fibers; shown here by injecting the vessels with dark plastic before sectioning.
endomysium capillary.where: Between the fibers of skeletal muscle.
endomysium capillary.fn: Supplies the high and very variable oxygen and substrate demand of working muscle and removes CO₂, lactate and heat.

erythrocyte.name: Erythrocyte (red blood cell)
erythrocyte.what: Anucleate biconcave disc about 7.2 µm across with no organelles; 30% of its content is haemoglobin.
erythrocyte.fn: Carries O₂ and CO₂. The biconcave shape increases surface area and lets the cell deform through capillaries; spectrin anchored by ankyrin gives the membrane its elasticity. Life span 120 days.

rouleaux.name: Rouleaux
rouleaux.where: Blood smears, especially where flow is slow or plasma proteins are high.
rouleaux.fn: A stacking artefact or a sign of raised plasma proteins; it also underlies a raised sedimentation rate.

sickle cell.name: Sickle cell
sickle cell.what: A crescent or sickle-shaped erythrocyte produced when deoxygenated HbS polymerizes.
sickle cell.where: Blood of patients with sickle cell disease.
sickle cell.fn: Rigid sickled cells block small vessels, causing pain crises and infarcts, and are destroyed early, causing haemolytic anaemia.

neutrophil.name: Neutrophil
neutrophil.what: The most numerous leukocyte; multilobed nucleus with fine, pale specific granules plus azurophilic (lysosomal) granules.
neutrophil.where: Blood, with a large reserve in bone marrow; migrates into connective tissue at sites of damage.
neutrophil.fn: First responder to tissue damage and the main killer of bacteria. Rolls on selectins, binds integrins, then migrates between endothelial cells; its specific granules hold lysozyme, collagenase, elastase and myeloperoxidase, and it uses the hexose monophosphate shunt for the respiratory burst.

eosinophil.name: Eosinophil
eosinophil.what: Bilobed nucleus with large, bright red-orange granules containing peroxidase, acid phosphatase and a core of major basic protein.
eosinophil.where: Blood and connective tissue; attracted by substances from basophils and mast cells.
eosinophil.fn: Kills helminths and other parasites, phagocytoses antigen–antibody complexes and neutralizes histamine. Numbers rise in allergy and parasitic infection.

basophil.name: Basophil
basophil.what: Bilobed nucleus usually hidden by large, intensely basophilic blue-purple granules.
basophil.fn: Granules contain heparin, histamine and SRS-A, and the cell carries IgE Fc receptors, so it releases histamine in allergic reactions and modulates inflammation.

lymphocyte.name: Lymphocyte
lymphocyte.what: Round cell with a dense round nucleus and a thin rim of pale blue cytoplasm; small, medium and large forms exist.
lymphocyte.where: Blood (about 30% of leukocytes), lymph and all lymphoid organs; recirculates between them.
lymphocyte.fn: The functional cell of the immune system: T cells (CD4 helper, CD8 cytotoxic) for cell-mediated immunity, B cells for antibody production, and NK cells. CD4 recognizes antigen on MHC II, CD8 on MHC I.

monocyte.name: Monocyte
monocyte.what: The largest leukocyte, with an indented or kidney-shaped nucleus and abundant grey-blue cytoplasm.
monocyte.where: Blood for only hours to a few days, then connective tissue.
monocyte.fn: Precursor of macrophages and other mononuclear phagocytes; phagocytoses debris and presents antigen.

platelet.name: Platelet (thrombocyte)
platelet.what: Small anucleate cell fragment with a pale hyalomere and a darker granulomere.
platelet.fn: Adheres to damaged vessel wall, aggregates and releases factors for clotting, plugging the breach and helping repair the vasculature.

plasma.name: Plasma
plasma.what: The fluid phase of blood; serum is plasma with the clotting elements removed.
plasma.fn: Carries the formed elements, proteins, nutrients and wastes. The volume percentage occupied by formed elements is the haematocrit.

blood smear.name: Blood smear
blood smear.what: A thin film of blood spread and stained (Wright or Giemsa) so individual formed elements can be identified and counted.
blood smear.fn: The standard way to identify red cells, each of the five leukocytes and platelets and to detect abnormal numbers or forms.

azurophilic granule.name: Azurophilic granules
azurophilic granule.what: Larger, darker granules that are the lysosomes of the cell; in neutrophils they hold phospholipase A, vitamin A binding proteins and collagenase.
azurophilic granule.fn: Digest material taken into the phagosome.

specific granule.name: Specific granules
specific granule.what: The smallest granules of the neutrophil, stained faintly.
specific granule.fn: Contain type IV collagenase, phospholipase, lysozyme, elastase and myeloperoxidase for killing and digesting bacteria and for crossing basement membrane.

reticulocyte.name: Reticulocyte
reticulocyte.what: An immature red cell released early from the marrow; supravital stain such as brilliant cresyl blue shows residual ribosomes as dark specks.
reticulocyte.fn: A count of how fast the marrow is producing red cells; raised after bleeding or haemolysis.

red bone marrow.name: Red bone marrow
red bone marrow.what: Stroma of collagen and reticular fibres in a three-dimensional network, with haemopoietic cords between wide sinusoids.
red bone marrow.where: Flat bones and the ends of long bones in the adult; the main site of blood formation after week 24 of gestation.
red bone marrow.fn: Produces millions of cells per day. Cell formation and differentiation take place on the cords, and mature cells cross into the sinusoids to enter the circulation.

sinusoid marrow.name: Marrow sinusoid
sinusoid marrow.what: A wide, thin-walled vascular channel connecting the arterial and venous sides within the marrow.
sinusoid marrow.fn: Forms the vascular compartment of the marrow; mature cells squeeze through its wall to leave for the blood.

pluripotent stem cell.name: Pluripotent stem cell
pluripotent stem cell.what: A self-replicating, self-sustaining cell that can give rise to every blood cell line.
pluripotent stem cell.fn: Some daughters stay as stem cells while others become colony-forming units that enter erythropoiesis, granulopoiesis or thrombopoiesis. This is the cell that makes bone marrow and cord blood transplants work.

erythroid precursor.name: Erythroid precursors
erythroid precursor.what: The maturation series from proerythroblast through basophilic, polychromatophilic and orthochromatophilic erythroblast; the cell and its nucleus shrink, the cytoplasm turns from blue to pink as haemoglobin accumulates, and the nucleus is finally extruded.
erythroid precursor.fn: Produce mature erythrocytes; recognising the direction of this colour change is the usual exam task.

granulopoiesis.name: Granulopoiesis
granulopoiesis.what: Myeloblast → promyelocyte (azurophilic granules appear) → myelocyte (specific granules appear) → metamyelocyte → band form → mature granulocyte.
granulopoiesis.fn: Produces neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils. The marrow holds a large reserve: stored cells outnumber circulating ones by about 16 to 1.

myelocyte.name: Neutrophilic myelocyte
myelocyte.what: The stage at which specific granules first appear while the nucleus is still round or oval; it is the last stage able to divide.
myelocyte.fn: Marks the commitment of the cell to the neutrophil line.

megakaryocyte.name: Megakaryocyte
megakaryocyte.what: A huge polyploid cell with a single large lobulated nucleus produced by endomitosis, and cytoplasm packed with demarcation membranes.
megakaryocyte.where: Red bone marrow, next to the sinusoids.
megakaryocyte.fn: Sheds its cytoplasm as platelets directly through the sinusoid wall; one cell yields thousands of platelets.

megakaryoblast.name: Megakaryoblast
megakaryoblast.what: The large basophilic precursor of the megakaryocyte, before the cytoplasm has developed demarcation membranes.
megakaryoblast.fn: Undergoes endomitosis (DNA replication without division) to become a megakaryocyte.

splenic macrophage.name: Splenic macrophage
splenic macrophage.what: A large phagocyte in the red pulp cords, often containing ingested erythrocytes and brown haemosiderin pigment.
splenic macrophage.where: Red pulp of the spleen (and liver).
splenic macrophage.fn: Removes aged, rigid or damaged red cells and recycles the iron — the spleen as the graveyard of the red cell.

tunica intima.name: Tunica intima
tunica intima.what: The innermost tunic: a simple squamous endothelium on a basal lamina, plus a subendothelial layer of loose connective tissue; bounded externally by the internal elastic lamina in arteries.
tunica intima.fn: The endothelium is a continuous non-thrombogenic lining that controls permeability, vascular tone and leukocyte traffic.

tunica media.name: Tunica media
tunica media.what: The middle tunic of concentric smooth muscle with variable elastic and collagen fibres; the layer that varies most between vessel types.
tunica media.where: All vessels except capillaries and the smallest venules.
tunica media.fn: Generates and maintains blood pressure. It is thick and elastic in elastic arteries, thick and muscular in muscular arteries, and thin in veins.

tunica adventitia.name: Tunica adventitia (externa)
tunica adventitia.what: The outer supporting coat of collagen and elastic fibres, containing vasa vasorum and nerves; separated from the media by the external elastic lamina in large arteries.
tunica adventitia.where: All vessels; it is the thickest layer in large veins.
tunica adventitia.fn: Anchors the vessel to surrounding tissue and carries its own blood and nerve supply.

endothelium.name: Endothelium
endothelium.what: A continuous simple squamous epithelium lining the entire cardiovascular system.
endothelium.where: Heart chambers, every blood vessel and the lymphatics.
endothelium.fn: A selectively permeable, antithrombogenic lining that also releases vasoactive substances and presents the selectins and adhesion molecules leukocytes use to leave the blood.

internal elastic lamina.name: Internal elastic lamina
internal elastic lamina.what: A wavy, refractile sheet of elastin at the outer edge of the intima, often thrown into folds in fixed tissue.
internal elastic lamina.fn: Its presence, with the external elastic lamina, is the histological hallmark used to identify an artery.

external elastic lamina.name: External elastic lamina
external elastic lamina.what: A sheet of elastin between the tunica media and the adventitia.
external elastic lamina.where: Muscular arteries, particularly obvious in larger ones.
external elastic lamina.fn: Marks the outer limit of the media and helps identify the vessel as an artery.

elastic artery.name: Elastic (conducting) artery
elastic artery.what: Large artery whose media is dominated by concentric fenestrated sheets of elastin between smooth muscle layers.
elastic artery.where: Aorta, innominate, common carotid, subclavian and most pulmonary arteries.
elastic artery.fn: Expands during systole and recoils during diastole, smoothing the pulsatile output of the ventricle into steady flow.

muscular artery.name: Muscular (distributing) artery
muscular artery.what: Artery with a thick media of smooth muscle and prominent internal and external elastic laminae.
muscular artery.fn: Distributes blood and regulates its delivery to organs by vasoconstriction and vasodilation.

arteriole.name: Arteriole
arteriole.what: Small artery with a narrow lumen and only one to three layers of smooth muscle in the media; no external elastic lamina.
arteriole.where: Just upstream of capillary beds everywhere.
arteriole.fn: The main resistance vessel: its smooth muscle tone sets peripheral resistance and therefore blood pressure and local flow.

capillary.name: Capillary
capillary.what: The smallest vessel: a single endothelial cell layer on a basal lamina, with pericytes but no media; lumen just wide enough for a red cell.
capillary.where: Between arterioles and venules in virtually every tissue.
capillary.fn: Site of all exchange of gases, nutrients and waste. Classified as continuous, fenestrated or sinusoidal.

continuous capillary.name: Continuous capillary
continuous capillary.what: Unbroken endothelium with tight junctions and a complete basal lamina; numerous pinocytotic vesicles.
continuous capillary.where: Muscle, nervous tissue, lung, skin, connective tissue.
continuous capillary.fn: The most selective type; in the CNS its tight junctions form the blood–brain barrier.

fenestrated capillary.name: Fenestrated capillary
fenestrated capillary.what: Endothelium perforated by pores (fenestrae), usually bridged by a thin diaphragm, with a continuous basal lamina.
fenestrated capillary.where: Endocrine glands, intestinal mucosa, renal glomerulus (there without diaphragms).
fenestrated capillary.fn: Allows rapid exchange of water and small molecules where fluid must move quickly.

sinusoidal capillary.name: Sinusoidal capillary (sinusoid)
sinusoidal capillary.what: Wide, irregular vessel with large gaps between endothelial cells, a discontinuous or absent basal lamina, and associated macrophages.
sinusoidal capillary.where: Liver, spleen, bone marrow, some endocrine organs.
sinusoidal capillary.fn: Permits exchange of proteins and even whole cells between blood and tissue; the slow flow gives macrophages time to screen the blood.

pericyte.name: Pericyte
pericyte.what: A contractile cell wrapped around the capillary, sharing its basal lamina.
pericyte.fn: Gives mechanical support, can regulate capillary diameter and acts as a progenitor during vessel repair.

venule.name: Venule
venule.what: Small vessel downstream of the capillary bed with a thin wall and a relatively large lumen; postcapillary venules have pericytes rather than a true media.
venule.fn: The main site at which leukocytes leave the blood, and where histamine makes the wall leaky during inflammation.

vein.name: Vein
vein.what: Vessel with a large flattened lumen, a thin media and a thick adventitia, often containing valves.
vein.where: Returning blood to the heart throughout the body.
vein.fn: Returns blood at low pressure; valves and the skeletal muscle pump prevent backflow.

venous valve.name: Venous valve
venous valve.what: Paired semilunar folds of intima projecting into the lumen.
venous valve.where: Medium-sized veins, especially of the limbs.
venous valve.fn: Ensures one-way flow toward the heart; incompetence produces varicose veins.

vasa vasorum.name: Vasa vasorum
vasa vasorum.what: Small arteries, veins and lymphatics running in the adventitia and outer media of a large vessel.
vasa vasorum.where: Adventitia of large arteries and veins.
vasa vasorum.fn: Supply the outer vessel wall, which is too thick to be nourished by diffusion from the lumen.

endocardium.name: Endocardium
endocardium.what: Innermost layer of the heart: endothelium on a thin subendothelial connective tissue layer, with a subendocardial layer that carries the Purkinje fibres.
endocardium.where: Lining all heart chambers and covering the valves.
endocardium.fn: A smooth, non-thrombogenic lining continuous with the intima of the great vessels.

myocardium.name: Myocardium
myocardium.what: The thick middle layer of cardiac muscle cells, thickest in the left ventricle.
myocardium.where: Wall of all four heart chambers.
myocardium.fn: The pump itself. Atrial cells also contain granules of atrial natriuretic hormone, released when the atrium is stretched, which makes the kidney excrete Na⁺ and water and lowers blood volume.

epicardium.name: Epicardium
epicardium.what: The outer layer: a mesothelium over loose connective tissue and fat that carries the coronary vessels and nerves.
epicardium.where: Outer surface of the heart, facing the pericardial cavity.
epicardium.fn: Its mesothelium faces the pericardial fluid and allows the beating heart to move without friction.

purkinje fiber.name: Purkinje fibre
purkinje fiber.what: Large, pale modified cardiac muscle cell with abundant glycogen and few myofibrils.
purkinje fiber.where: Subendocardial layer, forming the AV bundle of His and its branches.
purkinje fiber.fn: Conducts the impulse rapidly from the AV node to the ventricular myocardium so the ventricles contract from the apex upward.

sa node.name: Sinoatrial (SA) node
sa node.what: Small, pale cardiac muscle cells in a connective tissue matrix.
sa node.where: Wall of the right atrium at the upper end of the sulcus terminalis, near the entry of the superior vena cava.
sa node.fn: The pacemaker: it depolarizes spontaneously and sets the heart rate.

av node.name: Atrioventricular (AV) node
av node.what: Nodal tissue similar in appearance to the SA node.
av node.where: Inferior end of the interatrial septum.
av node.fn: Delays the impulse so the atria empty before the ventricles contract, then passes it to the bundle of His.

heart valve.name: Heart valve leaflet
heart valve.what: A core of dense collagen (fibrosa) covered on both faces by endocardium.
heart valve.where: Between atrium and ventricle and at the outflow of each ventricle.
heart valve.fn: Prevents backflow during the cardiac cycle; the collagen core carries the mechanical load.

lymphatic capillary.name: Lymphatic capillary
lymphatic capillary.what: Thin endothelial tube closed at one end, with loosely overlapping endothelial cells, an incomplete basal lamina and anchoring filaments tethering it to the surrounding tissue.
lymphatic capillary.where: Blind-ending in the connective tissue of most organs.
lymphatic capillary.fn: The overlapping cells act as valve-like flaps that open when interstitial pressure is high, letting fluid, protein, bacteria and cells enter and become lymph.

lymphatic vessel.name: Lymphatic vessel
lymphatic vessel.what: Thin-walled vessel with numerous valves, carrying clear, colourless lymph.
lymphatic vessel.where: Running from the tissues through lymph nodes to the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct, which empty into the subclavian veins.
lymphatic vessel.fn: Returns 2–4 L of fluid and a quarter to a half of plasma protein to the blood each day. Flow is driven by rhythmic contraction of the vessel, the skeletal muscle pump and the thoracic pump; obstruction causes severe oedema.

anchoring filament.name: Anchoring filaments
anchoring filament.what: Protein filaments tying the endothelial cells of a lymphatic capillary to the surrounding connective tissue.
anchoring filament.fn: When tissue fluid accumulates, they pull the endothelial flaps open so excess fluid drains into the capillary.

lymph node.name: Lymph node
lymph node.what: Small encapsulated bean-shaped organ with an outer cortex, a paracortex and a central medulla, set along lymphatic vessels.
lymph node.where: Along lymphatic vessels throughout the body, clustered in the neck, axilla, groin, mediastinum and mesentery.
lymph node.fn: Filters lymph and supports antibody production. Lymph enters through afferent lymphatics into the subcapsular sinus and leaves by the efferent lymphatic at the hilum.

capsule.name: Capsule
capsule.what: Dense connective tissue covering the organ, sending trabeculae inward.
capsule.fn: Supports the organ and carries vessels into it; afferent lymphatics pierce the capsule of a lymph node.

trabecula.name: Trabecula
trabecula.what: An extension of the capsule passing into the substance of the organ.
trabecula.fn: Divides the organ into compartments and carries blood vessels.

subcapsular sinus.name: Subcapsular (marginal) sinus
subcapsular sinus.what: The space just beneath the capsule, crossed by reticular fibres and macrophages.
subcapsular sinus.where: Lymph node, immediately under the capsule.
subcapsular sinus.fn: Receives lymph from the afferent lymphatics and distributes it to the cortical and medullary sinuses; macrophages here screen the lymph.

cortex node.name: Cortex (of lymph node)
cortex node.what: The outer zone packed with lymphatic nodules.
cortex node.where: Beneath the subcapsular sinus of a lymph node.
cortex node.fn: The B cell region; lymphatic nodules here enlarge and form germinal centres during an antibody response.

paracortex.name: Paracortex
paracortex.what: The deep cortex between the nodules and the medulla, diffusely filled with lymphocytes and containing high endothelial venules.
paracortex.where: Lymph node, between cortex and medulla.
paracortex.fn: The T cell region; lymphocytes enter the node from the blood here through the HEVs.

medulla node.name: Medulla (of lymph node)
medulla node.what: Pale central region of medullary cords separated by medullary sinuses.
medulla node.where: Centre of a lymph node, around the hilum.
medulla node.fn: Lymph drains through the sinuses to the efferent lymphatic; plasma cells in the cords secrete antibody into the lymph.

medullary cord.name: Medullary cord
medullary cord.what: A cord of lymphocytes, plasma cells and macrophages in the medulla.
medullary cord.fn: Plasma cells here release antibody into the lymph leaving the node.

medullary sinus.name: Medullary sinus
medullary sinus.what: Wide, irregular lymph channel between medullary cords, crossed by reticular fibres and macrophages.
medullary sinus.fn: Slows lymph flow so macrophages can phagocytose particles before the lymph leaves by the efferent vessel.

lymphatic nodule.name: Lymphatic nodule (follicle)
lymphatic nodule.what: A dense oval mass of lymphocytes; primary nodules are uniform, secondary nodules have a pale germinal centre and a dark mantle zone.
lymphatic nodule.where: Cortex of lymph nodes, white pulp of spleen, tonsils, Peyer patches and diffuse mucosal lymphoid tissue.
lymphatic nodule.fn: Site of B lymphocyte proliferation in response to antigen.

germinal center.name: Germinal centre
germinal center.what: Pale central zone of a secondary nodule containing large proliferating B lymphoblasts and macrophages.
germinal center.fn: Where B cells proliferate and mature into plasma cells and memory cells; its presence means the nodule is actively responding to antigen.

mantle zone.name: Mantle zone
mantle zone.what: The dark rim of small, tightly packed lymphocytes surrounding a germinal centre.
mantle zone.fn: Small resting B lymphocytes displaced to the periphery as the germinal centre expands.

high endothelial venule.name: High endothelial venule (HEV)
high endothelial venule.what: A postcapillary venule lined by unusually tall cuboidal endothelial cells.
high endothelial venule.where: Paracortex of lymph nodes, and in tonsils and Peyer patches.
high endothelial venule.fn: The doorway through which circulating lymphocytes leave the blood and enter the lymphoid organ, allowing continuous recirculation.

afferent lymphatic.name: Afferent lymphatic vessel
afferent lymphatic.what: Lymphatic vessel with valves that pierces the capsule on the convex surface of the node.
afferent lymphatic.fn: Brings lymph, antigen and antigen-presenting cells to the node; a node has several afferents but only one efferent.

efferent lymphatic.name: Efferent lymphatic vessel
efferent lymphatic.what: The single vessel leaving the node at the hilum.
efferent lymphatic.fn: Carries filtered, antibody-enriched lymph onward toward the thoracic duct.

reticular fiber.name: Reticular fibres and reticular cells
reticular fiber.what: A fine three-dimensional meshwork of type III collagen made by reticular cells; shown by silver impregnation.
reticular fiber.where: Stroma of lymph nodes, spleen, thymus and bone marrow.
reticular fiber.fn: Forms the scaffold that holds lymphocytes and macrophages in place and guides cell traffic through the organ.

spleen.name: Spleen
spleen.what: The largest lymphoid organ: a capsule and trabeculae enclosing white pulp around central arterioles and red pulp of cords and sinusoids.
spleen.fn: Filters blood rather than lymph: mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigen (white pulp) and removes worn-out red cells (red pulp). It has no afferent lymphatics.

white pulp.name: White pulp
white pulp.what: Periarteriolar lymphoid sheath of T cells around a central arteriole, with B cell nodules attached.
white pulp.fn: Immune surveillance of blood: antigen-presenting cells trap blood-borne antigen here and lymphocytes respond.

red pulp.name: Red pulp
red pulp.what: Splenic cords (of Billroth) of macrophages and blood cells, separated by wide venous sinusoids.
red pulp.where: Spleen, making up most of its bulk.
red pulp.fn: Old or damaged red cells are forced through the sinusoid wall; those too rigid to pass are phagocytosed by macrophages, which recycle the iron.

central arteriole.name: Central arteriole
central arteriole.what: A small artery running eccentrically through the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath.
central arteriole.fn: Identifies the white pulp in a section; it supplies the sheath and ends in the marginal zone and red pulp.

marginal zone.name: Marginal zone
marginal zone.what: The border region between white and red pulp, rich in macrophages and antigen-presenting cells.
marginal zone.fn: Where blood-borne antigen is first trapped and presented.

splenic sinusoid.name: Splenic sinusoid
splenic sinusoid.what: Wide vessel lined by elongated rod-like endothelial cells with gaps between them, encircled by hoop-like basal lamina.
splenic sinusoid.fn: Red cells must squeeze between the endothelial cells to re-enter the circulation; this is the test of deformability that removes aged cells.

thymus.name: Thymus
thymus.what: Encapsulated bilobed organ divided into lobules, each with a dark cortex and pale medulla; it involutes after puberty.
thymus.fn: The primary lymphoid organ where T lymphocytes mature and are selected; it has no afferent lymphatics and no lymphatic nodules.

thymic cortex.name: Thymic cortex
thymic cortex.what: Darkly stained outer zone densely packed with immature T cells among thymic epithelial cells.
thymic cortex.where: Outer part of each thymic lobule.
thymic cortex.fn: Where thymocytes proliferate and undergo selection; the blood–thymus barrier protects them from circulating antigen.

thymic medulla.name: Thymic medulla
thymic medulla.what: Pale inner zone with fewer, more mature lymphocytes and prominent epithelial cells.
thymic medulla.where: Centre of each thymic lobule, continuous between lobules.
thymic medulla.fn: Holds mature T cells about to leave for the blood, and contains Hassall corpuscles.

hassall corpuscle.name: Hassall (thymic) corpuscle
hassall corpuscle.what: A whorl of concentrically arranged, flattened and keratinizing epithelial reticular cells.
hassall corpuscle.fn: The defining feature used to identify the thymus in a section; associated with regulatory T cell development.

thymic epithelial cell.name: Thymic epithelial cell (TEC)
thymic epithelial cell.what: Pale, star-shaped epithelial reticular cell with long processes joined by desmosomes, enveloping the developing lymphocytes.
thymic epithelial cell.fn: Provides the framework (instead of reticular fibres), forms the blood–thymus barrier and presents self antigen during T cell selection.

tonsil.name: Tonsil
tonsil.what: Partially encapsulated mass of lymphoid tissue in the mucosa, with nodules under a surface epithelium that dips into crypts.
tonsil.where: Palatine (sides of the oropharynx), lingual (base of tongue) and pharyngeal tonsils (roof of nasopharynx).
tonsil.fn: Guards the entrance to the pharynx, sampling antigen from air and food; crypts increase the surface available for that sampling.

peyer patch.name: Peyer patch
peyer patch.what: A permanent cluster of lymphatic nodules in the mucosa and submucosa, covered by a dome epithelium containing M cells.
peyer patch.where: Ileum, at the junction of small with large intestine.
peyer patch.fn: Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue that samples gut antigen and mounts a local immune response.

m cell.name: M cell
m cell.what: A specialized epithelial cell with microfolds instead of microvilli, its basal surface pocketed around lymphocytes and dendritic cells.
m cell.where: Epithelium overlying Peyer patches and tonsils.
m cell.fn: Transports antigen and microorganisms from the lumen to the underlying lymphocytes and antigen-presenting cells.

appendix.name: Appendix
appendix.what: Blind tube off the caecum whose wall is crowded with lymphatic nodules in the mucosa and submucosa.
appendix.where: Right lower abdomen, attached to the caecum.
appendix.fn: Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue of the large intestine; the nodules often narrow or obliterate the lumen.

t lymphocyte.name: T lymphocyte
t lymphocyte.what: Lymphocyte carrying T cell receptors acquired in the thymus; no surface antibody. 60–80% of mature lymphocytes.
t lymphocyte.where: Blood, paracortex of lymph nodes, PALS of the spleen.
t lymphocyte.fn: Cell-mediated immunity. CD4 helper cells recognize antigen on MHC II and secrete IL-2; CD8 cytotoxic cells recognize antigen on MHC I and kill infected or tumour cells with perforin. HIV attacks CD4 cells.

b lymphocyte.name: B lymphocyte
b lymphocyte.what: Lymphocyte with surface immunoglobulin acting as its antigen receptor.
b lymphocyte.where: Blood, lymphatic nodules and germinal centres, medullary cords.
b lymphocyte.fn: Becomes a plasma cell that secretes antibody; T and B cells cannot be told apart by light microscopy alone.

plasma cell.name: Plasma cell
plasma cell.what: Oval cell with an eccentric clock-face nucleus and strongly basophilic cytoplasm from abundant rough ER.
plasma cell.where: Medullary cords of lymph nodes, connective tissue, and lamina propria.

slides.title: Skeletal muscle, longitudinal section
slides.desc: Long unbranched fibers with obvious cross-striations and flattened nuclei pushed to the periphery, just under the sarcolemma.

slides.title: Skeletal muscle, three preparations
slides.desc: Three views of skeletal muscle, including immunostaining, showing the regular striated pattern and peripheral nuclei.

slides.title: The three muscle types compared
slides.desc: Micrographs with matching drawings: (a) skeletal, multinucleated with peripheral nuclei; (b) cardiac, branched with intercalated discs and central nuclei; (c) smooth, fusiform cells with central nuclei and no striations.

slides.title: Muscle comparison table
slides.desc: Side-by-side comparison of skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle: fiber shape, striations, nuclei, T tubules, SR, junctions, control of contraction, connective tissue, locations, innervation and regeneration.

slides.title: Cardiac muscle
slides.desc: Branching striated fibers with single central nuclei, joined end to end by darkly stained intercalated discs.

slides.title: Cardiac muscle, ultrastructure
slides.desc: Electron micrograph showing the step-like intercalated disc with its transverse adhering junctions and longitudinal gap junctions, plus abundant mitochondria between myofibrils.

slides.title: Smooth muscle
slides.desc: Closely packed fusiform cells with single central nuclei and no cross-striations; the nucleus sits at the widest part of the cell.

slides.title: Smooth muscle, second view
slides.desc: Longitudinal and transverse profiles of smooth muscle; in cross section only some cells show a nucleus, because the nucleus occupies only the thickest part of each tapered cell.

slides.title: Smooth muscle ultrastructure, transverse
slides.desc: Electron micrograph of smooth muscle cut across: randomly arranged contractile filaments, dense bodies and surface caveolae instead of T tubules.

slides.title: Sarcomere, relaxed and contracted
slides.desc: Electron micrographs of one sarcomere before and after contraction, with Z discs, M line, H zone, A band and I bands marked. The A band keeps its length while the I band and H zone narrow.

hotspots.label: Z disc and M line after contraction

slides.title: Molecular organization of the sarcomere
slides.desc: Diagram of thick and thin filaments showing how their overlap creates the A band, I band, H zone, M line and Z discs.

slides.title: A and I bands, thick and thin filaments
slides.desc: Electron micrograph of the filament lattice: the A band where thick filaments lie, the zone of overlap with thin filaments, and the thin-filament-only I band.

slides.title: Transverse tubules and triads
slides.desc: Electron micrograph of T tubules flanked by terminal cisterns of sarcoplasmic reticulum, forming triads at the A–I junction of skeletal muscle.

slides.title: Neuromuscular junction
slides.desc: (a) Silver stain showing the nerve bundle (NB), motor end plates (MEP) on striated fibers (S); (b) SEM of the branching axon ending; (c) diagram of the end plate with synaptic vesicles of ACh, synaptic cleft and junctional folds of the sarcolemma.

slides.title: Capillaries of skeletal muscle
slides.desc: Blood vessels injected with dark plastic polymer before sectioning, revealing the rich capillary network in the endomysium around individual muscle fibers (×200, Giemsa with polarized light).

slides.title: Blood smear
slides.desc: A stained peripheral blood film, the standard preparation for identifying the formed elements of blood.

slides.title: Normal erythrocytes
slides.desc: Biconcave anucleate red cells about 7.2 µm across, some stacked as rouleaux; the pale centre is the thin part of the disc.

slides.title: Sickle cell erythrocytes
slides.desc: Crescent-shaped rigid red cells formed when deoxygenated haemoglobin S polymerizes.

slides.title: Neutrophils
slides.desc: The most numerous leukocyte: a multilobed nucleus with fine, pale specific granules.

slides.title: Neutrophil ultrastructure
slides.desc: Electron micrograph showing the lobed nucleus with the two granule populations: small specific granules and larger azurophilic granules (lysosomes) used to kill engulfed bacteria.

slides.title: Eosinophils
slides.desc: Bilobed nucleus with large bright red-orange granules, shown beside a lymphocyte for size comparison.

slides.title: Basophils
slides.desc: Large, intensely basophilic granules that obscure the bilobed nucleus.

slides.title: Lymphocytes
slides.desc: Round, dense nucleus with only a thin rim of pale cytoplasm; small, medium and large forms are present.

slides.title: Monocytes
slides.desc: The largest leukocyte, with an indented kidney-shaped nucleus and abundant grey-blue cytoplasm.

slides.title: Platelets
slides.desc: Small anucleate fragments of megakaryocyte cytoplasm, often clumped, with a pale hyalomere and darker central granulomere.

slides.title: Platelets, second view
slides.desc: Platelets among red cells in a smear, showing their small size relative to an erythrocyte.

slides.title: Leukocyte reference table
slides.desc: Reference table of the five leukocytes: nuclear shape, granules, percentage, life span and function.

slides.title: Red bone marrow active in haematopoiesis
slides.desc: Cellular haemopoietic cords between wide sinusoids, with fat cells interspersed; cells mature in the cords and cross into the sinusoids.

slides.title: Developing erythrocytes and granulocytes
slides.desc: Marrow smear showing erythroid cells with round dense nuclei alongside granulocytic cells at several stages of maturation.

slides.title: Major erythrocyte precursors
slides.desc: The erythroid series from proerythroblast to orthochromatophilic erythroblast: the cell shrinks, the nucleus condenses and is finally extruded, and the cytoplasm shifts from deep blue to pink as haemoglobin accumulates.

slides.title: Granulopoiesis
slides.desc: The granulocyte series: myeloblast, promyelocyte with azurophilic granules, myelocyte with specific granules, metamyelocyte, band form and mature neutrophil.

slides.title: Neutrophilic myelocyte
slides.desc: The stage at which specific granules first appear; it is the last dividing stage of the neutrophil line.

slides.title: Megakaryoblasts
slides.desc: Large basophilic precursors that will undergo endomitosis to become megakaryocytes.

slides.title: Megakaryocyte ultrastructure
slides.desc: Huge polyploid cell with a lobulated nucleus and cytoplasm subdivided by demarcation membranes into the territories that will be shed as platelets.

slides.title: Erythrocyte removal by splenic macrophages
slides.desc: Macrophages of the splenic red pulp containing ingested erythrocytes and iron pigment, removing aged and damaged red cells from the circulation.

slides.title: Tunics of the vascular wall
slides.desc: The three concentric coats common to all vessels: tunica intima with its endothelium, tunica media of smooth muscle and elastic fibres, and the outer adventitia.

slides.title: Walls of small arteries and veins
slides.desc: Labelled comparison of the layers: intima with endothelium and subendothelial layer, internal elastic lamina, media, external elastic lamina, adventitia and vasa vasorum.

slides.title: Elastic artery and vasa vasorum
slides.desc: An elastic artery whose media is filled with concentric elastic sheets, with vasa vasorum running in the adventitia to nourish the outer wall.

slides.title: Arterioles
slides.desc: Small arteries with a narrow lumen and only one to three layers of smooth muscle; the resistance vessels that control blood pressure.

slides.title: Capillaries and a muscular artery
slides.desc: Capillaries, seen as endothelial nuclei bulging into a narrow lumen, beside the thick smooth muscle wall of a muscular artery.

slides.title: Continuous capillary
slides.desc: Unbroken endothelium with tight junctions, a complete basal lamina and numerous pinocytotic vesicles.

slides.title: Fenestrated capillary
slides.desc: Endothelium perforated by fenestrae, usually closed by a thin diaphragm, over a continuous basal lamina.

slides.title: Sinusoidal capillary
slides.desc: A wide irregular vessel with gaps between endothelial cells and a discontinuous basal lamina, allowing proteins and whole cells to cross.

slides.title: Capillaries with pericytes
slides.desc: Electron micrograph of a capillary with a pericyte wrapped around it, sharing the capillary basal lamina.

slides.title: Microvasculature
slides.desc: The microcirculation: arteriole, capillary bed and postcapillary venule, where all exchange and most leukocyte emigration take place.

slides.title: Venules
slides.desc: Thin-walled vessels with relatively wide lumens draining the capillary bed; the main site at which leukocytes leave the blood.

slides.title: Veins
slides.desc: Large flattened lumen, thin media and a thick adventitia, in contrast with the thick muscular wall and round lumen of the accompanying artery.

slides.title: Wall of a large vein with a valve
slides.desc: A large vein with semilunar valve leaflets projecting into the lumen to keep blood moving toward the heart.

slides.title: Endocardium and myocardium
slides.desc: The endothelial lining and subendocardial layer, with Purkinje fibres, overlying the cardiac muscle of the myocardium.

slides.title: Epicardium
slides.desc: The outer layer of the heart: mesothelium over loose connective tissue and fat containing the coronary vessels and nerves.

slides.title: Heart valve leaflet
slides.desc: A dense collagenous core covered on both surfaces by endocardium.

slides.title: Lymphatic capillary
slides.desc: Diagram of a blind-ended lymphatic capillary: loosely overlapping endothelial cells form flap valves that open when interstitial pressure rises, with anchoring filaments tethering the vessel to the tissue.

slides.title: Lymphatic vessels with valves
slides.desc: Thin-walled lymphatic vessels containing valves that keep the low-pressure lymph flowing in one direction.

slides.title: Lymph node, overview
slides.desc: Labelled overview: capsule and trabeculae, subcapsular sinus, cortex with lymphatic nodules and germinal centres, paracortex with high endothelial venules, and medulla of cords and sinuses, with afferent vessels entering and the efferent leaving at the hilum.

slides.title: Regions of the lymph node
slides.desc: Low power view showing the three regions in order from the capsule inward: cortex, paracortex and medulla.

slides.title: Lymph node cortex
slides.desc: Densely packed lymphatic nodules beneath the subcapsular sinus, the B cell region of the node.

slides.title: Lymph node cortex and paracortex
slides.desc: The nodular cortex above and the diffuse T cell paracortex below, where high endothelial venules admit circulating lymphocytes.

slides.title: Lymph node medulla
slides.desc: Pale medullary cords of lymphocytes, plasma cells and macrophages separated by wide medullary sinuses.

slides.title: High endothelial venules
slides.desc: Postcapillary venules lined by tall cuboidal endothelial cells, with lymphocytes caught in the act of crossing into the node.

slides.title: Lymphoid nodules (follicles)
slides.desc: Primary and secondary nodules; the secondary nodule has a pale germinal centre of proliferating B cells ringed by a dark mantle zone.

slides.title: Reticular fibres and cells
slides.desc: Silver impregnation showing the three-dimensional meshwork of reticular fibres that supports the lymphocytes of lymphoid tissue.

slides.title: Receptors on T and B lymphocytes
slides.desc: T cells carry T cell receptors with CD4 or CD8; B cells carry surface immunoglobulin. CD4 reads antigen on MHC II, CD8 on MHC I.

slides.title: Spleen
slides.desc: Capsule and trabeculae with islands of white pulp scattered through the dark red pulp.

slides.title: White pulp of the spleen
slides.desc: Periarteriolar lymphoid sheath of T cells around an eccentric central arteriole, with an attached B cell nodule.

slides.title: Red pulp of the spleen
slides.desc: Splenic cords packed with red cells and macrophages, separated by wide venous sinusoids.

slides.title: Structure and function of splenic sinusoids
slides.desc: Rod-like endothelial cells with gaps between them: red cells must deform to squeeze back into the circulation, and those that cannot are removed by macrophages.

slides.title: Blood flow in the spleen
slides.desc: The route of blood: trabecular artery, central arteriole in the white pulp, marginal zone, then the cords and sinuses of the red pulp.

slides.title: Thymus
slides.desc: Lobules separated by connective tissue septa, each with a dark, lymphocyte-packed cortex and a pale medulla.

slides.title: Cortex of the thymus
slides.desc: Pale star-shaped thymic epithelial cells with long processes surrounding densely packed developing T lymphocytes.

slides.title: Thymic medulla with Hassall corpuscles
slides.desc: Pale medulla containing whorls of concentrically arranged keratinizing epithelial cells — the feature that identifies the thymus.

slides.title: Tonsils
slides.desc: Lymphoid tissue beneath a surface epithelium that dips into deep crypts; the diagram shows the pharyngeal, palatine and lingual tonsils guarding the pharynx.

slides.title: Peyer patch and M cells
slides.desc: Clusters of nodules in the ileal wall under a dome epithelium containing M cells, which ferry antigen from the lumen to lymphocytes and dendritic cells held in their basal pockets.

slides.title: Appendix
slides.desc: A narrow lumen surrounded by mucosa and submucosa crowded with lymphatic nodules.

slides.title: Lymphoid organ reference table
slides.desc: Comparison of thymus, lymph node, spleen and MALT: capsule, nodules, lymphatic vessels and unique features such as Hassall corpuscles, medullary cords and crypts.
